name: Ponpon Mania
studio: Patrick Heng (creative development) and Justine Soulié (art direction/illustration)
techniques: illustrated panels packed into WebGL texture atlases and reconstructed as shaded planes in an ogl scene
custom shader cross-fade between whole pages, timed by GSAP tweens
GSAP SplitText line-by-line dialogue reveals
spring-physics mouse-repulsion on background elements (clouds)
Matter.js physics on the About page
palette: mostly black-and-white comic panels; color is withheld and only appears inside dream sequences, so it reads as a narrative cue rather than decoration
type: comic lettering paired with a music-player-style chapter UI (tracks, not chapters), reinforcing the sheep protagonist's DJ ambition
motion: GSAP timelines drive scroll-synced panel reveals while a bespoke shader blends one whole page into the next like a deck transition, and background elements flee the cursor under spring physics
why: choosing ogl over three.js and treating every hand-drawn panel as a shader-mapped texture-atlas plane is how a full illustrated comic stays smooth without shipping a heavy scene graph per page

name: Cartier Watches & Wonders 2025
techniques: six discrete three.js scenes, one alcove per emblematic watch, each staged like its own spotlit installation
Blender-authored geometry and materials streamed into the WebGL scenes
Lenis-smoothed scroll driving camera movement between alcoves
hidden clickable gestures inside each 3D scene that unlock further detail
Web Audio-threaded ambient score synced to scene transitions
palette: near-black per-alcove grounds, each lit in a single warm accent pulled from that watch's own material (gold, lacquer, gem)
type: restrained serif wordmark and small-caps labels kept subordinate to the 3D staging, functioning as museum signage rather than a headline
motion: scrolling physically moves the camera through a sequence of self-contained 3D rooms instead of sliding 2D sections, so the site behaves like a walkthrough of the trade-fair pavilion it is modeled on
why: treating the whole site as architecture - discrete rooms you walk between - rather than a stack of hero sections is the move worth taking whenever a brief has more than one hero product to feature

name: Montfort
techniques: WebGL 3D transitions between the four business-division sections (Trading, Capital, Maritime, Fort Energy)
swipe/scroll-driven card rotation for the CSR pillars section
gesture-driven hover micro-interactions throughout
palette: two-color system only - a deep petrol blue (#29648e) against near-white (#f4f6f8), chosen to keep a commodities-trading brand legible instead of decorative
type: clean corporate sans across large section headers and dense body copy, sized for a text-heavy financial-services brief
motion: scroll and swipe prompts carry the visitor through modular, 3D-transitioned cards for each business line, smoothed by Lenis rather than snapping between states
why: the craft here is restraint - a two-color palette and a small number of exact 3D transitions used to organize a genuinely dense corporate site instead of dressing it up

name: Siena Film Foundation
studio: Niccolò Miranda (design & technical direction), production by G-NS Studio, development by Federico Valla
techniques: WebGL-powered horizontal filmstrip slider for the homepage and project archive
subtle parallax on poster imagery as the strip scrolls, reading as physical depth rather than a CSS transform
card-based film sections with festival-accolade and critical-quote overlays
palette: dark cinematic ground with high-contrast white type; each film's own poster grading (warm for one title, cool blue for another) supplies the only color variation
type: clean sans-serif for headlines and metadata, vintage-poster-inspired display treatment inside the slider itself, a repeated star-icon motif punctuating review quotes
motion: one WebGL filmstrip shared by the homepage and archive scrubs horizontally like an actual reel, parallaxing each poster against its caption as it passes
why: building the slider itself in WebGL rather than CSS transforms is what makes the filmstrip conceit - posters parallaxing like frames under a loupe - read as a real material instead of a carousel plugin

name: Lando Norris
techniques: real-time WebGL 3D rotation across the multi-year helmet archive
Rive-driven vector motion layered over the 3D helmet work
speed-themed scroll-triggered transitions between race and helmet sections
palette: near-black ground cut with a single lime-green accent, pushed for maximum contrast rather than blended in
type: bold contemporary sans for headlines against smaller refined body copy; the lime accent does typographic as well as decorative work
motion: scrolling spins and steps through a hall-of-fame of Norris's own helmet designs (2019-2025) in real 3D, while Rive handles the smaller kinetic-type flourishes around it
why: reaching for real-time 3D specifically because the subject has fifteen-plus genuine yearly variants (the helmets), rather than one hero product, is what turns a driver-bio site into a collection you rotate through

name: KODE Immersive
techniques: custom shader logic and ambient lighting built for cross-browser/device performance testing
cursor-reactive interactions layered over the 3D scene
run-together, no-space display copy ('Withthehelpoftechnology') used as a typographic effect
palette: dark charcoal/black ground with white text and selective bright accents, tech-forward rather than warm
type: sans-serif in varying weights, deliberately unconventional word-spacing on key display lines to slow the reading rhythm
motion: a numbered service breakdown ('00123 Ideate') and prev/next scroll cues move the visitor through the studio's own capability pitch inside the same real-time 3D shell it sells to clients
why: removing spaces from a display line is a cheap typographic trick that reads as expensive next to a genuinely shader-driven scene, because it signals the same confidence as the 3D work rather than fighting it

name: Iventions
techniques: a three.js scene used for atmosphere and framing rather than spectacle - each project staged like a spotlit installation
GSAP-paced reveals that turn the page into a guided walkthrough instead of a grid
palette: not independently confirmed beyond the spotlight concept - dark staging grounds implied by the installation framing
type: bold identity typography paired with motion-led UX, per the studio's own positioning as an event-architecture brand
motion: scrolling paces revealed installations one at a time, the three.js lighting doing the work of a spotlight moving across a stage rather than a hero animation looping for attention
why: using three.js as stage lighting - dimming and framing real photography - rather than as the subject itself is the reusable idea for any portfolio whose actual work is physical, not digital

name: Messenger
studio: Abeto (developed by Vicente Lucendo and Michael Sungaila, music by Kevin Colombin)
techniques: a small spherical planet rendered and navigated in real time, cel-shaded low-poly style
GPU-driven physics, lighting and animation for the delivery character and world
WebSocket-based multiplayer so other players' couriers are visible and emoji-reactive live on the same planet
palette: saturated cel-shaded color per planet biome, a Jet Set Radio-adjacent palette rather than a corporate brand system
type: minimal in-world UI type, the game deliberately keeps chrome out of the way of the 3D planet itself
motion: the whole experience is a playable, spinning 3D planet - the courier runs, jumps and delivers packages across its compact geography while other live players' avatars move in the same shared instance
why: winning Awwwards' Developer Site of the Year with a literal browser game rather than a marketing site is the proof point that a real-time WebGL world, not a scroll effect, is what the top developer prize actually rewards

name: basement.studio
techniques: three.js scene built with React (open-sourced on GitHub) rather than a raw WebGL/GLSL pipeline
case-study-led homepage (Vercel Ship, Daylight, KidSuper, Shop MrBeast) instead of a project grid
palette: not independently confirmed in detail beyond a dark, tech-studio ground consistent with the studio's client roster
type: plain-spoken, lower-case brand voice ('we make cool shit that performs') carried into blunt sans-serif headline type
motion: not independently confirmed beyond the 3D homepage scene; the studio's own positioning leads with performance and craft over spectacle
why: open-sourcing the exact three.js/React site that won the award is a rare case where the technique claims can be checked line by line instead of taken on faith

name: Fiddle.Digital - The New Us
techniques: a WebGL context pool running multiple canvases in parallel so several small effects share one resource budget
a noise-based algorithm assigning colors that a WebGL shader maps onto mosaic icons, with per-cell fade rates creating a trail effect
an in-house animation module suite (StringTune) handling smooth scroll, FPS tracking, lazy loading, parallax and cursor interaction at a fixed 60fps target
an audio-reactive vinyl-scratch effect on the About page
zero-transition, deliberately abrupt cuts used as a page-transition choice
palette: minimalist, high-contrast palette built around a redesigned mascot ('Susuwatari') as the sole illustrative accent
type: clean modern sans throughout, restrained rather than expressive, letting the mosaic and mascot carry the personality
motion: cursor position drives a grid of shader-mapped icons directly, so pointer movement reads as material interaction rather than a hover state
why: running several lightweight WebGL canvases through one shared context pool, instead of one large three.js scene, is the pattern worth copying whenever a page needs many small living details rather than one big hero

name: Roman Jean-Elie - Portfolio '25
techniques: WebGL 'fold' effect using manual vector projection to bend DOM-aligned geometry
MeshPortal rendering via FBO/render targets to show a second scene through a shape
GSAP MorphSVG driving path morphs, rendered through a canvas-optimized pipeline
velocity-based shader distortion tied to scroll speed
DOM-to-WebGL bounds synchronization so 3D elements track real layout
palette: dark, near-monochrome ground built around black silhouettes, letting embedded client video and character animation supply the only color
type: a single bold display face (Anton) carrying section titles, set large enough to double as a shape the WebGL fold effect can bend
motion: a three-step hover timeline (Cinema 2008, Theater 2013, Code 2020) narrates the developer's own path before the project grid loads, and scroll velocity itself feeds the shader distortion on transitions
why: letting scroll speed itself become a shader uniform - so faster scrolling visibly stretches the distortion - ties the motion directly to user input instead of running on a fixed timeline

name: Altitude 101
techniques: a three.js 3D hero section positioning a traditional film-production studio's rebrand toward immersive/Apple Vision Pro work
palette: not independently confirmed - Metabole's own case study focuses on strategic positioning over palette specifics
motion: not independently confirmed beyond the 3D hero itself
why: reaching for three.js specifically to signal a production studio's pivot from flat video work to immersive/spatial content makes the technology choice part of the pitch, not just decoration
